name: F-statistic
seoDesc: F-statistic: work out total number of coefficients (K) from the sample variance #2 and the sum square of residuals — full model. A free statistics…
summary: The F-statistic calculator solves for total number of coefficients (K). The inputs are the sample variance #2, the sum square of residuals — full model, the sum square of residuals — restricted model and number of excluded coefficients. That makes it useful for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the F-statistic calculator work?
sections.html:
The F-statistic calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total number of coefficients (K) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the test type); then you type in the sample variance #2 (S₂^2), the sum square of residuals — full model (SSRF), the sum square of residuals — restricted model (SSRR) and number of excluded coefficients (J).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the F-statistic calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Total number of coefficients (K)=(f-statistic (F) × sum square of residuals — full model (SSRF) × number of excluded coefficients (J) + sum square of residuals — full model (SSRF) × sample size (N) − sum square of residuals — restricted model (SSRR) × sample size (N)) ÷ (sum square of residuals — full model (SSRF) − sum square of residuals — restricted model (SSRR))
Sample variance #1 (S₁^2)=f-statistic (F) × sample variance #2 (S₂^2)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Test type set to Multiple regression, Sample variance #2 (S₂^2) = 10 and F-statistic (F) = 10. The calculator returns Sample variance #1 (S₁^2) = 100.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Sample variance #1 (S₁^2) = 100 should be roughly the size you expected from Test type set to Multiple regression and Sample variance #2 (S₂^2) = 10.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The F-statistic calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the sample variance #2, the sum square of residuals — full model and the sum square of residuals — restricted model — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the F-statistic calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total number of coefficients (K), derived from the sample variance #2, the sum square of residuals — full model and the sum square of residuals — restricted model. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the F-statistic calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the sample variance #2, the sum square of residuals — full model, the sum square of residuals — restricted model and number of excluded coefficients, which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Sample variance #1 (S₁^2) = 100. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the F-statistic calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
